Maintainable code is good code. Code that nearly any programmer can jump into maintaining or extending is good code. When programmers forego fanciness for understandability, other programmers who will maintain that code won't need to spend long hours deciphering what the original coder's mindset was and why they wrote it the way they did. Also, using repeatable patterns, even if they are not the widespread patterns used by many, will make the code easier to parse and understand. Good comment conventions that explain unusual or complicated functions/features are far better than relying on the programmer to parse the code blind. Coding smarter by removing the reliance on error handling by changing the mode of the operations so that most errors cannot even materialize is also a major indicator of good code. You don't have to out-think your idiot users if you never let them get into trouble in the first place!

I've been programming for nearly three decades and have developed my own flavor of maintainable coding. I have taught many fledgling programmers these techniques and it has vastly improved their code's maintainability. Having a strong OOP background and a penchant for patterns, my code is often broken into the smallest functional units I can make that are not too atomic or bloated and confusing. This allows for other programmers to quickly understand my object models and how they can reuse them anywhere in the code. I have gotten to the point where I have written code generators that make well fleshed out stub code that follows my style which cuts my coding time down by heaps. I will admit that reaching this level of patterned programming sometimes makes things boring and monotonous, but the robustness and stability of my code often pays off in spades. I have left quite a few systems behind at various companies I have worked for in the past that are alive and growing today. I don't consider them legacy since they are still being added to so that must mean I did a pretty good job of making it maintainable and understandable. It's pretty awesome to know some of my "children" are still going strong even though I'm not around to raise them.

Code that can't be read, is code that will eventually be replaced. Don't strive for maximum complexity, strive for maximum readability. Don't do things that will surprise the next guy who has to maintain it.
